reason: The court held that only the Bank's discretionary third question under Finance Act section 71(3) was immune, but the statement omits that statutory and jurisdictional frame.
The general settlement principle was accepted, but the court actually upheld setting aside this settlement because the court was misled and a non-party municipal interest was affected.
The court treated those three elements as the basic ingredients of the actio locati in deciding whether arrears of rent had been proved.
The rent-agreement point was ratio, but the statement omits the material context of enhanced rent, demand, agreement, and possible inferred agreement by continued occupation.
The court described the landlord's attempted shift from damages to rent as a litigation fact, not as a legal rule permitting such a switch.
The case did not establish the tautological rule stated; the promissory-note point was at most a case-specific finding and the appeal turned on the Trusts Ordinance analysis.
The court held that a good-faith purchaser for value could not be subjected to specific performance through section 93 of the Trusts Ordinance.
The duty point was part of the holding, but the statement omits the Forest Ordinance permit context, bona fide exercise of discretion, appropriate circumstances, and loss-causing breach.
The court found permit refusal caused loss here, but only because the withholding was unreasonable and amounted to a negligent breach of statutory duty in the circumstances.
The court identified signature by the party making the deed as one essential element of due execution under section 2 of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance.
The court held that once section 2 execution requirements were met, a false or wrong execution date inserted by the notary did not void the deed.
The notary-prosecution point was an ancillary observation after deciding deed validity, not a necessary holding between the parties.
The court rejected the handwriting expert's opinion because the comparison signatures and related material had not been proved genuine.
The court's point was the opposite in this case: delay meant the trial judge could not reasonably rely on remembered credibility and demeanour.
The will-proof rule was ratio, but the statement omits the material conditions about testamentary capacity, absence of suspicious circumstances, and the propounder's burden if suspicion arises.
The court relied on Evidence Ordinance sections 91 and 92 to reject evidence varying a simple notarial transfer into a mortgage or retransfer agreement.
The court held on the facts that the daughter's Urban Council rent deposits were made on behalf of the tenant father and attracted section 21 of the Rent Act.
The deemed-receipt rule was ratio, but only for rent deposited with the authorised local authority under section 21 of the Rent Act, which the statement omits.
The court treated security for an interim injunction as security against compensation that may be ordered under section 667 of the Civil Procedure Code.
The section 667 point was a holding, but the statement drops the two situations that define the rule.
The case concerned compensation and security after an injunction application, not a standalone rule that injunctions should not be granted on insufficient grounds.
The court held that the rent receipts, read with their references to Edwin Fernando's lease, did not establish a tenancy for Appuhamy.
The burden point was ratio, but the statement omits the rei vindicatio context where ownership was admitted and the defendant had to prove his asserted right to remain.
The section 93 trust holding was real, but the statement omits the material requirements that the contract be specifically enforceable and, for immovable property, duly registered to give notice.
The probate rules were ratio, but the extracted statement is too vague to state any of the actual rules or conditions the court applied.
